content: Penicillin G potassium is an antibiotic approved by the FDA for the treatment of serious infections caused by susceptible strains of specific microorganisms. These infections include septicemia, empyema, pneumonia, pericarditis, endocarditis, meningitis, anthrax, actinomycosis, botulism, diphtheria, erysipelothrix, fusospirochetosis, and others. Common adverse reactions to Penicillin G potassium include hypersensitivity reactions, hemolytic anemia, nausea, vomiting, stomatitis, neutropenia, hyperreflexia, seizures, interstitial nephritis, and thrombophlebitis. For adults, Penicillin G sodium for injection is indicated for serious infections caused by susceptible organisms. Before initiating treatment, appropriate culture and susceptibility tests should be performed to identify the causative organism and its sensitivity to Penicillin G. Therapy may begin before test results are available if there is a strong suspicion of infection by susceptible organisms. Once results are available, therapy should be adjusted accordingly. To prevent the development of drug-resistant bacteria, Penicillin G sodium should only be used for infections proven or strongly suspected to be caused by susceptible bacteria. Dosage adjustments may be necessary for patients with hepatic or renal impairment. For most acute infections, treatment should continue for at least 48 to 72 hours after the patient becomes asymptomatic. For Group A β-hemolytic streptococcal infections, therapy should be maintained for at least 10 days to reduce the risk of rheumatic fever. Penicillin G sodium can be administered intravenously or intramuscularly. Solutions should be prepared by loosening the powder in the vial, adding diluent slowly against the vial wall, and shaking vigorously. Penicillin solutions should not be mixed with carbohydrate solutions at alkaline pH, as this rapidly inactivates the drug. Off-label uses supported by guidelines include treatment of Lyme disease and prophylaxis for Group B Streptococcus infections in infants during labor. There is limited information on non-guideline-supported off-label uses in adults. In pediatric patients, Penicillin G potassium should not be administered in doses less than one million units. Dosages are generally weight-based and should be calculated individually. Newborns with incompletely developed renal function may require dosage and frequency adjustments. All newborns treated with penicillins should be closely monitored for clinical and laboratory evidence of toxicity or adverse effects. Penicillin G potassium is contraindicated in patients with a history of hypersensitivity (anaphylactic) reactions to any penicillin. Immediate allergic reactions, such as anaphylaxis, are rare but can occur, particularly after parenteral administration. Delayed reactions, such as fever, rash, and arthralgia, may occur one to two weeks after therapy initiation. Pseudomembranous colitis has been reported during or after treatment. High doses of Penicillin G sodium may cause electrolyte disturbances, congestive heart failure, neurotoxic reactions (e.g., seizures, coma), and renal tubular damage. Discontinuation of the drug usually resolves these reactions. Penicillin G is excreted in human milk, so caution should be exercised when administering it to nursing mothers. In pregnancy, Penicillin G is classified as Category B by the FDA, indicating no evidence of harm to the fetus in animal studies, but adequate human studies are lacking. It should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. Pharmacokinetically, Penicillin G is rapidly cleared by the kidneys through glomerular filtration and active tubular secretion. Renal clearance is delayed in premature infants, neonates, and the elderly due to reduced renal function. In cases of renal impairment, dosage adjustments are necessary. Probenecid can prolong the elimination of Penicillin G by blocking renal tubular secretion. Penicillin G is distributed to various tissues, including the lungs, liver, kidneys, and placenta. Its penetration into the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) improves with inflamed meninges, achieving CSF/serum ratios of 2-6%. Hemodialysis can reduce serum levels of Penicillin G. Penicillin G is bactericidal against susceptible microorganisms during active multiplication by inhibiting cell wall synthesis. It is not effective against penicillinase-producing bacteria, such as many strains of staphylococci. It is highly active against certain streptococci, pneumococci, and Neisseria meningitidis. However, it is no longer the drug of choice for infections caused by some gram-negative bacilli, such as Escherichia coli and Proteus mirabilis. Storage of Penicillin G sodium dry powder should be at 20°-25°C (68°-77°F). Reconstituted sterile solutions can be refrigerated (2°-8°C) for up to three days without significant loss of potency.
